introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les deux questions de la Section Three.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (cohérence et organisation, présentation claire de la problématique, thèse, antithèse, synthèse et conclusion) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) sans barème chiffré par partie ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question (Q5 : 5 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 25 ; Q6 : 5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25) : aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), code 0790, JUNE 2023, trois heures.

Q4 : Tempels (« Bantu Philosophy », ouvrage de référence ; ontologie de la force vitale, hiérarchie Dieu, ancêtres, vivants, animaux, plantes, minéraux, influence entre forces) exposé en grandes lignes ; les critiques (Hountondji, Towa, Wiredu, Eboussi Boulaga) et les prolongements (Kagame et ses catégories muntu, kintu, hantu, kuntu, nuance par rapport à Tempels, Mbiti, Senghor) suivent la classification courante ; l'origine luba de l'enquête de Tempels est le repère généralement admis. Aucune citation littérale, aucune date, aucun numéro de page ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie. Le sujet imprime « force-being » entre guillemets ; recopié.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The notion of "force-being" is central in African metaphysics. Justify this claim.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (problematic).** Metaphysics asks what exists and what it is to be. In *Bantu Philosophy* the Belgian missionary Placide Tempels argued that the Bantu understand being not as a static substance (as in much Western thought) but as *force*: to be is to have vital force, and every being is a force. This is the idea of "force-being". The claim to justify is that this notion is central in African metaphysics. The problem is whether force-being really is the key to African thought on reality, or only one interpretation, valid for some peoples and open to criticism.

**Thesis: force-being is central to African metaphysics.**
- *A dynamic ontology.* For Tempels, being is force, and force is being: reality is not made of inert things but of living forces that act, grow and diminish. This explains the African view that the world is alive and that nothing is purely material.
- *A hierarchy of forces.* Beings are ordered: God, the creator and source of all force; the ancestors; living humans (chiefs and elders, then others); animals and plants; and, last, minerals and inanimate things. Each lower force depends on the higher ones.
- *Interaction and unity of the cosmos.* Forces influence one another: a stronger force can strengthen or weaken a weaker one, so the universe is a network of relations in which the visible and invisible, the living and the dead are linked. This agrees with holistic African conceptions found by Mbiti and others (the unity of the religious and the profane, the continuity between generations).
- *Basis for ethics, religion and social life.* Good is what increases vital force (life, health, fertility, harmony); evil is what diminishes it. Rites, taboos, respect for elders, ancestors and the sacred, and the work of the healer all aim to preserve and strengthen life. Force-being thus connects metaphysics with ethics, religion and politics.
- *Echoes in other thinkers.* Alexis Kagame's study of Kinyarwanda categories (human beings, things, place and time, modality) developed an African ontology from language, and he is usually read as refining Tempels. Senghor's presentation of African reason as participation, with its emphasis on life and rhythm, also resonates with the dynamic vision.

**Antithesis: the notion is neither universal nor beyond criticism.**
- *Generalisation.* Tempels drew his conclusions mostly from one Bantu people (the Luba) and extended them to "the Bantu" and sometimes to Africa; Africa has many peoples and metaphysical systems. Other themes also appear central: time and the person (Mbiti), destiny and the person (Akan and Yoruba thought), the pairing of the visible and invisible world.
- *Western imposition.* Hountondji and Towa argue that "force-being" reads African beliefs through Western categories, and that Tempels addressed colonial missionaries and administrators, not Africans; he did not test his claims by critical dialogue with the people concerned.
- *Linguistic issues.* Wiredu and others note that questions about "being" depend on the structure of a language; in some African languages there is no single word covering "being" as Western metaphysics defines it, so the equation of being with force may be a construction.
- *Unanimism.* Presenting one ontology as shared by an entire people neglects individual thinkers and disagreement, the main reproach of Hountondji against ethno-philosophy.

**Synthesis.** Force-being is best taken as a central *interpretive model* of many African worldviews, not as the single and complete metaphysics of Africa. It captures real features (the vitality of the cosmos, the hierarchy and interdependence of beings, the link between metaphysics and ethics), and it has opened the debate about African ontology. It should be tested by critical study of each tradition, with comparison and attention to language.

**Conclusion.** The claim is justified to a large extent: force-being gives a coherent and influential account of reality, humanity, society and morality in the thought of several African peoples, and it has shaped the whole discussion of African metaphysics. It is not exhaustive: it reflects Tempels' reading of the Bantu and needs correction by other African ontologies and by critical philosophy. Its importance lies in showing that African traditions raise genuine metaphysical questions with an original answer.
